query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn HEA, removal of Co increases the intrinsic lattice distortion and modestly lowers the effective stacking fault energy compared to CoCrFeMnNi. This altered landscape enhances dislocation‐solute interactions, thereby promoting a dynamic strain aging mechanism (manifested as pronounced serrated flow and intermittent work hardening) at intermediate temperatures and strain rates. At high strain rates, the diminished contribution from phonon drag (owing to reduced Co-mediated bonding characteristics) results in a relatively lower jump in dynamic yield strength, thereby preserving a favorable strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, homogenized single‐phase solid solution FeNiCrMn HEA (Co‐free) with a uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to a series of controlled mechanical tests (e.g., split-Hopkinson pressure bar or high-strain-rate tensile/compressive tests) over a matrix of temperatures (room temperature to ~700 °C) and strain rates (from ≈10^−3 s^−1 up to >10^3 s^−1), while concurrently performing in situ microstructural characterization (e.g., high-speed imaging, synchrotron X-ray diffraction or high resolution TEM on deformed specimens).
generation.conditions: Testing temperatures between RT and 700 °C; strain rates spanning from quasi‐static (~10^−3 s^−1) to dynamic regimes (>10^3 s^−1).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion that intensifies dislocation pinning/unpinning interactions (dynamic strain aging) and affects twin nucleation events.
generation.mechanism: The increased lattice distortion due to the absence of Co elevates the sensitivity of dislocations to local solute atmospheres, facilitating frequent pinning and abrupt unpinning events (i.e. dynamic strain aging). This produces measurable serrations and sustained work hardening at intermediate strain rates. Meanwhile, without Co, the typical high-strain-rate strengthening imparted by phonon drag is reduced, leading to a moderated dynamic yield strength jump.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the well-studied CoCrFeMnNi baseline, the Co‐free FeNiCrMn HEA is expected to exhibit: (a) more pronounced serrated flow and higher amplitude stress drops at intermediate strain rates/temperatures (indicative of dynamic strain aging); (b) a delayed or less abrupt yield strength jump at very high strain rates because of reduced phonon drag; and (c) overall, a dynamic balance that sustains a high work hardening rate to maintain strength–ductility trade‐offs.
generation.baseline: Dynamic mechanical and microstructural behavior of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA as reported in previous studies (e.g., those examining phonon drag induced yield jumps and dislocation pinning/unpinning serration phenomena).
generation.boundary: This mechanistic explanation applies within the temperature range up to approximately 700 °C and strain rates between ≈10^−3 s^−1 and >10^3 s^−1. Beyond these boundaries (e.g., in regimes where dynamic recrystallization or recovery dominates), additional mechanisms may prevail.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings on phonon drag effects observed in Co-containing HEAs (PMC7512474::web::013::4_1_the_constitutive_model_and_strain_ra) and serration/dynamic strain aging models (PMC4655315::web::009::model_assumptions) by extrapolating that the removal of Co shifts the interplay between these mechanisms. Uncertainties remain in how exactly the altered lattice parameters and solute interactions affect stacking fault energy and dislocation mobility; in situ microstructural evidence under dynamic loading is needed to fully validate the proposed mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of Co‐free FeNiCrMn HEA and another of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA (baseline), ensuring identical processing and microstructural states. Perform dynamic deformation tests across the specified temperature and strain-rate matrix. Use in situ diagnostics (such as high-speed synchrotron X-ray diffraction and high-resolution TEM on interrupted tests) to capture stress–strain curves and microstructural evolution (dislocation configurations, twin density, etc.).
measurements: Stress–strain curves with emphasis on serration amplitude and work hardening rate at intermediate strain rates.
Dynamic yield strength jumps and their evolution with increasing strain rate.
In situ microstructural metrics (dislocation density, twin formation frequency) correlated with stress serrations.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co‐free FeNiCrMn HEA does not exhibit significantly more pronounced serration behavior and a distinct work hardening profile (relative to the Co-containing baseline) at intermediate strain rates/temperatures, or if its dynamic yield strength jump is not reduced as predicted, then the hypothesis that enhanced dynamic strain aging (modulated by lattice distortion changes due to Co removal) is the dominant mechanism must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: For HEAs, the model assumes that weak spots are weakened even further upon slipping to model how dislocations break free from the surrounding pinning atoms. This assumption is reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier (PLC) effect or dynamic strain aging. The weak spots re-heal to their original strength during the time between avalanches at a material-specific healing rate, Λ. Specifically, after a weak spot has slipped, the local failure stress, τf,l, drops from its initial value, τs,l, to a lower value, τd,l, by an amount given by the weakening parameter, ε (τs,l − τd,l)/τs,l. It remains at this weakened value until the slip avalanche is completed. Afterwards, τf,l is increased to its initial value, τs,l, at the temperature-dependent healing rate, Λ, until the weak spot slips again during a new avalanche, and the process repeats. The re-strengthening of the weak spots models the rearrangement of atoms around arrested dislocations, leading to the (re-)“pinning” or anchoring of stationary dislocations in place. cited_evidence.text: The NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy had positive activation volume at strain rates less than 1 × 10−2 s−1. However, when the specimen deformed under high strain rates (beyond 1 × 103 s−1), the deformation time was very short. There was not enough time available for thermal energy to help dislocations overcome the barriers. The NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy had a different deformation mechanism at dynamic loading. According to the literature [], the large jump in yield strength at high strain rates is probably due to the phonon drag effect on the motion of dislocations. The phonon drag phenomenon becomes very effective during plastic deformation at high strain rates []. A phonon is an elastic lattice vibration propagating in a crystal []. The viscous drag generating from the interaction of the dislocations has negative impacts on the deformation progress. The drag effects by the phonons can be ignored under quasi-static conditions for low dislocation velocities. However, high dislocation velocities under high strain rates would enhance the phonon drag effects greatly and lead to phonons scattering, which also hinders dislocation movement.
